coverage: Nine stories · cybersecurity, robots, transportation, science, education and streaming

cards.headline: Researchers use AI tools to find OpenAI security flaws
cards.summary: Hacktron AI researchers used AI coding tools while testing OpenAI under its bug-bounty program. They reached employee accounts and software resources, reported the flaws instead of taking code, and OpenAI says it fixed the vulnerabilities.
cards.whyItMatters: AI can speed up defensive security work as well as attacks. Responsible disclosure gives researchers a legal way to find problems and help organizations repair them before criminals exploit them.

csp.connection: The same computing tools can have beneficial or harmful effects depending on how people use them.

cards.headline: Anthropic brings AI experiments into a real biology lab
cards.summary: Anthropic confirmed that it has built a Bay Area wet lab for physical biology experiments as it expands its life-science work. The company is also exploring ways for Claude to direct laboratory robots, while saying human oversight remains essential.
cards.whyItMatters: AI is moving beyond text and images into experiments with physical equipment. Combining software, robotics and biology could change how scientists test ideas and search for new treatments.

csp.connection: Computing innovations can combine with other fields and change how scientific work is performed.

cards.headline: Training robot brains takes lots of real-world motion data
cards.summary: Spirit AI says better software and training data are now major bottlenecks for useful humanoid robots. About 1,000 contractors collect examples of everyday human motions that the company uses to train robots for physical tasks.
cards.whyItMatters: A robot needs more than motors and sensors. Like other machine-learning systems, its behavior depends heavily on the examples used to train its software.

csp.connection: Machine-learning systems use collected data to learn patterns that influence later behavior.

cards.headline: Waymo plans self-driving rides in Singapore
cards.summary: Waymo says it plans to launch an all-electric autonomous ride-hailing service in Singapore by 2028, its first Southeast Asian market. Human specialists will first drive the vehicles so the system can adapt to local roads and monsoon weather.
cards.whyItMatters: Self-driving software has to work in many environments, not just one city. Roads, weather, laws and local driving patterns all become inputs to designing and testing the system.

csp.connection: Computing systems interact with physical environments and must be tested for the conditions where people will use them.

cards.headline: A carmaker wants to sell its software to other brands
cards.summary: Chinese electric-vehicle maker Xpeng plans to offer other automakers technology including cockpit systems, AI chips and driver-assistance software. The strategy treats a modern car's computing platform as something that can be shared separately from the vehicle brand.
cards.whyItMatters: Cars increasingly behave like networked computer systems on wheels. Hardware architecture, chips and software can become reusable platforms much like technology inside phones and laptops.

csp.connection: Complex products combine hardware and software layers that can be designed as reusable systems.

cards.headline: Disney puts one leader over streaming and ad technology
cards.summary: Disney named Adam Smith chairman of its streaming business, covering services such as Disney+ and Hulu. His responsibilities also include the company's advertising technology and emerging technologies as streaming becomes more central to how Disney distributes entertainment.
cards.whyItMatters: Watching a show feels simple, but streaming depends on software for subscriptions, recommendations, delivery and advertising. Entertainment companies increasingly organize around those computing systems.

csp.connection: Digital platforms change how media is distributed and how organizations build services around users.

cards.headline: A new look at how deeply schools depend on Big Tech
cards.summary: A New Yorker analysis examines how platforms from Google, Microsoft and Apple became basic infrastructure for many U.S. schools. It connects that dependence with cybersecurity, student-data privacy and current debates about how much AI and screen technology belong in classrooms.
cards.whyItMatters: School technology is not neutral background equipment. Choosing platforms affects privacy, security, learning and what happens when a system goes offline.

csp.connection: Computing choices can create tradeoffs involving privacy, access, reliability and social effects.

cards.headline: A robot builds and tunes a laser experiment by itself
cards.summary: MIT researchers built a robotic optics lab that can arrange mirrors and lenses, tune them with micron-scale precision and repair alignment after disturbances. In a demonstration, it assembled a working laser cavity through 50 autonomous moves in about 30 minutes.
cards.whyItMatters: Automation can handle repetitive precision work while scientists focus on questions and results. The project combines robotics, sensors, QR-coded data and software into one physical computing system.

csp.connection: A complete computing system can coordinate software, sensors, stored data and physical devices to perform a task.

cards.headline: Satellite data shows Lake Powell at a record low
cards.summary: NASA Earth Observatory reports that Lake Powell reached record-low water levels after low mountain snow and unusual warmth reduced runoff into the Colorado River system. Scientists track the reservoir using Landsat satellite imagery along with measurements on the ground.
cards.whyItMatters: Computing turns repeated satellite observations into a record of environmental change. Comparing data across time helps scientists measure trends that are difficult to see from one observation alone.

csp.connection: Large datasets collected over time can be processed and compared to identify meaningful changes in the physical world.
